title: Superposition & Bridges
description: Add up the effect of each source separately, and measure resistance with a balanced bridge.

study.title: Superposition principle
study.body: In a **linear** circuit (resistors, linear dependent sources and independent sources) every voltage and current is the sum of the contributions of the independent sources, each acting alone with the other independent sources set to zero. Keep the same reference direction for every partial result and add them with their signs.

study.title: Zeroing sources
study.body: A voltage source set to zero is a **short circuit**; a current source set to zero is an **open circuit**. Dependent sources are **never** zeroed: they stay in every sub-circuit. In the circuit shown, $V_s$ alone gives a voltage divider and $I_s$ alone sees $R_1 \parallel R_2$:

study.title: Power does not superpose
study.body: Power is proportional to the **square** of current or voltage, so the power of the sum is not the sum of the powers. Superpose currents or voltages first, then compute the power.

study.title: When superposition helps
study.body: Superposition pays off when each one-source sub-circuit is a simple divider or series/parallel problem, and for understanding how an output depends on each input (e.g. a summing network). With many sources, node or mesh analysis is usually faster because it solves everything at once.

study.title: Wheatstone bridge
study.body: Four resistors form two voltage dividers fed by $v_s$, with a sensitive detector between their midpoints a and b. Precision resistors are adjusted until the detector shows **zero current**: the bridge is **balanced**, $i_g = 0$ and $v_{ab} = 0$. Then $R_1 R_x = R_2 R_3$, so the unknown resistance follows without needing a calibrated meter.

study.title: Unbalanced bridge
study.body: With the detector removed, each side is a voltage divider. A small change in $R_x$ (e.g. a strain gauge) gives a small $v_{ab}$, often only millivolts. Seen from a–b the bridge has Thévenin resistance $R_t = R_1 \parallel R_3 + R_2 \parallel R_x$, which sets the detector current.

steps.title: Superposition
steps.body: In a linear circuit with several independent sources, any voltage or current is the **sum** of the responses to each source acting alone. To let one source act alone, set all other independent sources to zero.

steps.prompt: When you set an independent **voltage** source to zero, you replace it by…
options: a resistor equal to its internal resistance
steps.explanation: A zero voltage source keeps 0 V between its terminals while passing any current, which is exactly a wire (short circuit). A zero current source passes 0 A at any voltage: an open circuit.

steps.prompt: Find the part $v'$ of the voltage $v$ across $R_2$ (+ at the top) that is due to $V_s$ alone.
steps.hint: Set $I_s$ to zero: which element replaces it?
steps.explanation:
Zero $I_s$ → open circuit. Then $R_1$ and $R_2$ form a simple voltage divider:
$v' = V_s\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$ = {{Vs}} × {{R2/1e3}}/{{(R1 + R2)/1e3}} = **{{v1|V}}**

steps.prompt: What happens to each item when you apply superposition?
steps.explanation: Independent sources are zeroed (voltage → short, current → open), dependent sources stay active, and power must be computed from the **total** current or voltage.

steps.prompt: The power in a resistor can be found by adding the powers caused by each source acting alone.
steps.explanation: False. $P = R i^2$ is not linear. Example: two sources each causing 1 mA in a 1 kΩ resistor (same direction) give 2 mA in total, so $P$ = 4 mW, not 1 + 1 = 2 mW. Add the currents first, then square.

steps.title: Wheatstone bridge
steps.body:
The Wheatstone bridge measures an unknown resistance $R_x$. Adjust the known resistors until the detector between a and b shows zero current. In that **balanced** state $v_a = v_b$, which gives
$$ R_x = \frac{R_2}{R_1}\,R_3 $$

steps.prompt: The bridge is balanced with $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}}, $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}} and $R_3$ = {{R3|Ω}}. Find $R_x$.
steps.explanation:
At balance $v_a = v_b$: $\frac{R_3}{R_1 + R_3} = \frac{R_x}{R_2 + R_x}$, which simplifies to $R_1 R_x = R_2 R_3$.
$R_x = \frac{R_2}{R_1}R_3$ = ({{R2|Ω}} / {{R1|Ω}}) × {{R3|Ω}} = **{{R2*R3/R1|Ω}}**

steps.prompt: Which condition holds when this bridge is balanced?
steps.explanation: Balance means equal divider ratios on both sides: $\frac{R_3}{R_1 + R_3} = \frac{R_x}{R_2 + R_x}$, equivalently $\frac{R_1}{R_3} = \frac{R_2}{R_x}$. Cross-multiplying gives $R_1 R_x = R_2 R_3$: the products of **opposite** arms are equal.

steps.prompt: Find the part $v''$ of the voltage $v$ across $R_2$ (+ at the top) that is due to $I_s$ alone.
steps.explanation:
Zero $V_s$ → short circuit. $R_1$ now also goes from the top node to the bottom wire, so $I_s$ flows into $R_1 \parallel R_2$:
$v'' = I_s\,(R_1 \parallel R_2)$ = {{Is|A}} × {{Rp|Ω}} = **{{v2|V}}**

steps.prompt: Find the total voltage $v$ across $R_2$ (+ at the top).
Use superposition to find the node voltage $v$.
steps.hint: With one source shorted, the other sees a voltage divider with two resistors in parallel.

steps.prompt: Same circuit: find only the contribution $v''$ of $V_{s2}$ to $v$.
steps.explanation:
Short $V_{s1}$: then $R_1$ and $R_3$ are in parallel from node $v$ to the bottom, $R_1 \parallel R_3$ = {{par(R1, R3)|Ω}}. Divider with $R_2$:
$v'' = V_{s2}\frac{R_1 \parallel R_3}{R_2 + R_1 \parallel R_3}$ = {{Vs2}} × {{par(R1, R3)|Ω}} / {{R2 + par(R1, R3)|Ω}} = **{{vb|V}}**

steps.prompt: A bridge has $R_1$ = 1 kΩ fixed. It balances with the range resistor $R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}} and the dial $R_3$ = {{R3|Ω}}. Find $R_x$.
steps.explanation: $R_2/R_1$ = {{R2/1000}} is the range multiplier, and $R_x = \frac{R_2}{R_1}R_3$ = {{R2/1000}} × {{R3|Ω|4}} = **{{R2*R3/1000|Ω|4}}**. Changing $R_2$ by decades lets one dial cover many orders of magnitude.

steps.prompt: The detector is removed. Find $v_{ab} = v_a - v_b$ for $v_s$ = {{Vs|V}} (it may be negative).
A bridge is balanced. Then $R_x$ increases slightly (say, a strain gauge is stretched). What happens to $v_{ab} = v_a - v_b$?
steps.explanation: $v_a = v_s R_3/(R_1 + R_3)$ does not change. $v_b = v_s R_x/(R_2 + R_x)$ grows when $R_x$ grows, because $R_x$ takes a larger share of $v_s$. So $v_a - v_b$ goes from 0 to a negative value.

steps.prompt: When applying superposition, dependent sources are zeroed in the same way as independent sources.
steps.explanation: False. Only **independent** sources are switched off one at a time. A dependent source reacts to the voltages and currents in each sub-circuit, so it remains in every sub-circuit.

steps.prompt: You use superposition to find the part of the response caused by $V_{s1}$ alone. Tap every source you must set to **zero**. (The diamond is a dependent source controlled by the current $i_x$ through $R_2$.)
steps.explanation:
Superposition turns off the **other independent** sources: $V_{s2}$ becomes a short circuit and $I_s$ an open circuit.
The dependent source $\beta i_x$ stays in the circuit: it is not an input, it describes how the circuit behaves (like a resistor does). It responds to whatever $i_x$ the active source produces.

steps.prompt: Find the contribution of $I_s$ alone to the current $i_4$ (downward through $R_4$).
steps.explanation:
Short $V_s$. Then $R_1 \parallel R_2$ = {{par(R1, R2)|Ω}} hangs from the left end of $R_3$, so $I_s$ sees two paths to the bottom: $R_4$, and $R_3 + R_1 \parallel R_2$ = {{Rl|Ω}}.
Current divider: $i_4'' = I_s\frac{R_3 + R_1 \parallel R_2}{R_3 + R_1 \parallel R_2 + R_4}$ = {{Is|A}} × {{Rl|Ω}} / {{Rl + R4|Ω}} = **{{i4b|A}}**

steps.prompt: Now find the total current $i_4$ (downward through $R_4$).
The values are shown in the schematic. Tap the resistor you could remove **without changing any other current** in the circuit.
steps.explanation:
This is a Wheatstone bridge. Check the balance condition:
$$\frac{R_1}{R_2} = \frac{1\text{ k}\Omega}{2.2\text{ k}\Omega} = \frac{10\text{ k}\Omega}{22\text{ k}\Omega} = \frac{R_3}{R_4}$$
So both middle nodes are at the same voltage, $V_s\cdot\frac{2.2}{3.2}$ = 6.875 V, and $R_5$ has 0 V across it: it carries no current. Removing it changes nothing. Removing any other resistor would upset the balance and change the currents.

steps.prompt: With the detector removed, find the Thévenin resistance of the bridge seen from a–b.
steps.explanation:
Zero $v_s$: the top and bottom wires become the same node. From a, $R_1$ and $R_3$ both go to that node (parallel); from there $R_2$ and $R_x$ both go to b (parallel):
$R_t = R_1 \parallel R_3 + R_2 \parallel R_x$ = {{par(R1, R3)|Ω}} + {{par(R2, Rx)|Ω}} = **{{par(R1, R3) + par(R2, Rx)|Ω}}**

steps.prompt: A detector with resistance $R_g$ = {{Rg|Ω}} is connected between a and b. Find the detector current from a to b (it may be negative).
A strain-gauge bridge has $R_1 = R_2 = R_3 = R$ = {{R|Ω}} and the gauge $R_x = R + \Delta R$ with $\Delta R$ = {{dR|Ω}}. With $v_s$ = {{Vs|V}}, find $v_{ab} = v_a - v_b$.
steps.explanation:
$v_a = v_s\frac{R}{2R} = \frac{v_s}{2}$ = {{Vs/2|V}} and $v_b = v_s\frac{R + \Delta R}{2R + \Delta R}$ = {{Vs*(R + dR)/(2*R + dR)|V|5}}.
$v_{ab} = -\frac{v_s\,\Delta R}{2(2R + \Delta R)}$ = **{{Vs*(0.5 - (R + dR)/(2*R + dR))|V}}**
A tiny resistance change gives only millivolts, which is why the bridge output is usually amplified.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of a superposition solution in order.
items: Keep one independent source, zero all others
Replace zeroed voltage sources by shorts and current sources by opens
Solve the simple circuit for the wanted quantity
Add the partial results with their signs
steps.explanation: Each pass solves a one-source circuit with the same reference direction for the unknown. Only after all passes are the partial voltages or currents added; compute power only from the total.
